text: Derive the UTF-8 encoding of the character é, which is code point U+00E9. Give the binary fills as digit strings and the hex fills as two digits each.
choices: U+00E9 in binary is 1110 1001, which needs 8 bits, so UTF-8 uses two bytes.
The two-byte form is 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx, holding 11 payload bits: 00011101001
explanation: 11000011, 10101001, C3, A9 — matching the bytes the previous program printed. The structure is worth noticing: the leading bits of the first byte say how many bytes follow, and every continuation byte begins 10. That makes UTF-8 a prefix code (Chapter 33) and self-synchronizing, so a decoder that lands mid-character can find the next boundary by scanning forward for a byte that does not start with 10.
